newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian relief crew embrace weary comrades on Mir.
newsitem.headline: Russian relief crew embrace weary comrades on Mir.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts embraced the weary, accident-prone crew of the crippled Mir space station on Thursday after a difficult docking of their Soyuz spacecraft.
Live television pictures showed the cosmonauts smiling and hugging after hatches were opened at 1830 GMT, as scheduled, bringing relief to the three-man Russian-U.S. crew aboard Mir.
Pictures showed them floating in Mir's weightlessness, working on cables and securing bolts as they made final touches to the link-up. There was no clear sound.
The relief crew had to dock manually after automatic systems developed a fault 13 metres (yards) from Mir, Flight Director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters.
"Soyuz retreated by 25 metres and then docked manually," he said. "It was a technical malfunction. The situation was not a critical one but we will look into it."
Despite the hitch, Russia's top space official said repair works should go well.
Applause burst out at the tense Mission Control outside Moscow and a huge sign "Congratulations" appeared on the screen after the docking at 1702 GMT, a minute ahead of schedule.
"The docking went well. We are in a good mood. Today we saw a new stage in space epics," a smiling Yuri Koptev, head of Russia's Space Agency, told reporters.
"I am satisfied. The docking went perfectly," added Marshal Yevgeny Shaposhnikov, President Boris Yeltsin's space and aviation adviser.
Commander Anatoly Solovyov, 49, and 43-year-old flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov are facing a daunting task of restoring power to the ageing station.

Mir suffered its worst accident on June 25, when a supply ship pierced its Spektr scientific module during a manual docking manoeuvre. Cosmonauts had to unplug power cables leading from Spektr's solar panels as they fled the module and sealed it. The accident deprived Mir of up to half of its power supply.
Solovyov and Vinogradov will don space suits on August 20 and enter the airless, darkened Spektr to reconnect the cables.
"The crew which has arrived at Mir is perfectly trained and I think they'll be able to fulfil all the tasks," Koptev said.

The next major task for the new crew would be to locate and fix the puncture in the Spektr and Koptev said up to six space walks had been scheduled for the operation. But he added that the crew might well be able to cope in two or three sorties.
NASA astronaut, British-American physicist Michael Foale is due to take part in a space walk scheduled for September 3 with the new Mir commander, Solovyov, to find the hole in the Spektr.
The two Russians on Mir, including commander Vasily Tsibliyev who has a stress-induced heart problem, are to return to Earth on August 14. Foale will stay until late September.
Probably the most immediate problem the joint crew will face is oxygen supplies. The current crew earlier on Thursday failed to fix the Elektron system and said more time would be needed.
They are now burning oxygen "candles", the only oxygen source on Mir when it started orbiting the Earth 11 years ago.
"The cosmonauts will come back to the search for the malfunction once the docking is fully over," Koptev said. "But I can tell you one thing, oxygen reserves (without Elektron) will last 70 days."
